name: Familial Juvenile Hypertrophy of the Breast

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Familial Juvenile Hypertrophy of the Breast

criteria.description: Rapid, excessive, and symmetrical breast enlargement during puberty
Positive family history of juvenile breast hypertrophy
Histological confirmation showing stromal and glandular hyperplasia without malignancy
Normal or mildly elevated estrogen and progesterone levels
Exclusion of other causes of breast enlargement such as tumors or endocrine disorders

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of rapid symmetrical breast enlargement during puberty with positive family history and histopathological confirmation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by family history and histopathology; hormonal studies assist in excluding other causes.

searchTerms: massive breast enlargement on both sides

pathognomonic.symptomName: Familial occurrence of juvenile breast hypertrophy
searchTerms: family history of early breast overgrowth

common.symptomName: Skin stretching with possible striae formation
searchTerms: skin tightness and striae on breasts

common.symptomName: Postural back pain due to breast weight
searchTerms: posture problems due to breast weight

common.symptomName: Psychological distress related to breast size
searchTerms: psychological issues related to breast size

occasional.symptomName: Ulceration or skin breakdown due to macromastia

searchTerms: mild hormone imbalance like high estrogen
reduced range of motion in shoulders

rare.notes: Due to maceration under large breasts

searchTerms: localized edema due to lymphatic obstruction

rare.symptomName: Nerve compression symptoms such as paresthesia
searchTerms: numbness or tingling from nerve pressure

laboratory: Normal or mildly elevated serum estrogen and progesterone levels
Exclusion of endocrine tumors or systemic causes
imaging: Ultrasound showing diffuse glandular and stromal hypertrophy without discrete masses
MRI may be used to exclude neoplastic lesions
genetic: Familial inheritance pattern suggesting autosomal dominant transmission
other: Histopathology showing stromal and glandular hyperplasia without atypia or malignancy

distinguishingFeatures: Possible association with hormonal therapy or pregnancy
Histology showing benign tumor rather than diffuse hypertrophy

redFlags: Rapid unilateral breast enlargement suggesting malignancy
Ulceration or necrosis of breast tissue
Severe psychological distress or depression related to body image
references: Orphanet: Familial Juvenile Hypertrophy of the Breast (ORPHA:180176)
Schwartz, R. A., & Janniger, C. K. (2005). Juvenile gigantomastia: a review. Pediatric Dermatology, 22(3), 260-263.
Khan, S., & Al-Hadithy, N. (2017). Juvenile hypertrophy of the breast: a review of the literature. Annals of Plastic Surgery, 78(3), 335-339.
